articleSummary: June saw Australia's first confirmed cases of high-pathogenicity avian influenza H5N1, a virus that has killed millions of wild birds, farmed poultry and marine mammals, with human infections remaining rare but hundreds of deaths globally. The book traverses from Melbourne to Mongolia, Edmonton to Indonesia, and from North Queensland to Fairbanks, Alaska, interviewing virologists, birdwatchers, ecologists, wildlife carers and citizen scientists. Dulaney frames spillover against drivers such as habitat destruction, climate change, the wildlife trade and industrial capitalism, arguing these forces push pathogens toward humans. The Hendra virus outbreak in Queensland is linked to bats displaced by deforestation; Alaskapox/Borealpox is connected to warming, deforestation and urban expansion. He warns of a coming global health crisis requiring proactive action.

articleSummary: Vietnam reports severe Japanese encephalitis among children, with cases admitted to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. A 9-year-old from Lao Cai presented with fever and headache, rapidly progressed to coma, respiratory failure, and required intubation and mechanical ventilation. After about two weeks of intensive care, consciousness improved and ventilation was stopped, but he remained weak and at risk of neurological sequelae, including epilepsy; recovery requires ongoing monitoring for impaired motor function and cognitive issues. Early symptoms are non-specific and may resemble common viral infections, complicating timely diagnosis. Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne viral infection that peaks in Vietnam during hot, humid summer. There is no specific antiviral treatment; care is supportive, including anti-edema, seizure prevention, and respiratory support. About half of survivors experience long-term neurobehavioral sequelae. Authorities urge full vaccination, vector control, and prompt medical evaluation for fever with altered mental status or seizures.

Previously affected provinces include Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Upper Uele, and Tshopo. A death in Lower Uele occurred in a traveler from Upper Uele. As of now, the outbreak has reached 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths, about three months after the declaration. The 2018–2020 outbreak remains the deadliest, with roughly 3,500 cases and about 2,300 deaths. Ebola spreads via bodily fluids and causes hemorrhagic fever.

articleSummary: Yellow fever outbreak in Brazil (2017–2018) tied to unprecedented drought, per Science Advances study led by Jamie Coldwell of Princeton University. The team found the dry spell inverted the usual rainfall-driven spread, with 1,376 infections and 483 deaths across the country over two years. The disease reached large cities in Minas Gerais as drought forced monkeys to migrate to urban areas for water, carrying the virus to Haemagogus forest mosquitoes that then moved into cities and transmitted it to Aedes aegypti. Yellow fever is a mosquito-borne virus, with about 90% of cases occurring in Africa; severe illness features high fever, organ damage, and bleeding, and roughly half of those progressing to severe disease die within 7–10 days. The study warns recurring droughts could heighten the risk of new urban outbreaks in major cities.
notes: 記事は2017-2018年の過去の流行を分析した研究成果の紹介であり、現時点での新規アウトブレイクや進行中の公衆衛生上の脅威を報告するものではない。将来的な干ばつによる都市部アウトブレイクのリスクについて言及しているが、これは研究上の警告であり、現在の具体的イベントではない。

articleSummary: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), a tick-borne viral infection caused by Dabie bandavirus, is entering China's high-risk season. Since April 1, 2026, SFTS is a Category B disease under the national Infectious Diseases Law. Shandong is among seven high-risk provinces (Anhui, Henan, Hubei, Liaoning, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) with peak transmission April–October, mainly affecting older rural farmers and outdoor workers. Early symptoms mimic a cold but include fever (38–40°C), fatigue, myalgia, loss of appetite, nausea, diarrhea, and progressive thrombocytopenia and leukopenia. Severe illness can involve bleeding, confusion, dyspnea, and oliguria. Transmission is primarily through tick bites; secondary spread can occur via contact with infected blood, secretions, or animals (cattle, sheep, cats, dogs). Prevention emphasizes protective clothing, DEET, permethrin-treated gear, body checks, and environmental cleanup. After a bite, avoid burning or oiling the tick; remove with tweezers, disinfect, and monitor for two weeks.
notes: 本記事は季節性のSFTS注意喚起であり、具体的な患者数・死亡数などの新規アウトブレイク情報は含まれていない。中国では2026年4月よりSFTSが法定伝染病B類に指定され、山東省含む7省が高リスク地域とされている。ヒトーヒト感染（血液・分泌物経由）のリスクも言及されており、季節推移を注視する必要がある。

articleSummary: Severe falciparum malaria linked to Africa travel persists in Vietnam, with Artesunate shared from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City to save lives. Bach Mai Hospital treated several imported cases and facilitated a 1,700+ km overnight transport of Artesunate to Ho Chi Minh City when local stock ran out, aided by a WHO donation. A 32-year-old Thanh Hóa man, who previously worked in Angola (July 2024–July 2025) and recently moved between Hà Tĩnh and Cat Hai Island, Hai Phong, developed high fever on August 5, with hypotension and severe thrombocytopenia. He was diagnosed with severe malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum with renal and hepatic failure; after transfer to Bach Mai, fever subsided and clinical status improved by August 11. Earlier, a 23-year-old Nghệ An woman who had lived in Nigeria presented August 1 with fever; diagnosed with P. falciparum malaria and recovered. Vietnam reports over 100 imported malaria cases annually, with more than 10 domestic cases, underscoring the need for travel-history diligence in febrile patients.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak has spread to Bas-Uele, the sixth province affected in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A death was confirmed in Buta, Bas-Uele, in a patient who traveled from Isiro, Haut-Uele, by motorbike taxi. As of August 14, total confirmed Ebola cases reached 4,665 with 2,184 deaths (case fatality ~46.8%). Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for about 90% of cases and 80% of deaths. The outbreak is progressing faster than previous waves; delayed case detection, ongoing armed conflict, and an overburdened health system hinder response and enable transmission. Bas-Uele borders South Sudan and the Central African Republic, and the Haut-Uele–Basu-Uele case shows spread along population routes. Africa CDC urges international support to deploy Ervebo; Kinshasa has requested 100,000 doses for trials, frontline workers, and high-risk groups. Ervebo targets Ebola Zaire; experts say it may offer protection and reduce mortality even with Bundibugyo in this outbreak.
